teaser.text: TJX Companies is a retailer built around the pleasure of finding a bargain. It buys clothing, home goods, and other everyday merchandise, sells most of it through stores below comparable full-price prices, and tries to keep the difference after the costs of running that system.

stock.title: TJX stock forecast
stock.meta_description: TJX's forecast weighs bear, base and bull scenarios, then tests store growth, margins, cash generation and valuation.
stock.opening: TJX's weighted path reaches $156.84 in October 2029, after outcomes ranging from $115.98 to $191.65. It hinges on whether TJX can grow stores and baskets without giving back its value advantage.
stock.closing: The full TJX memo also explains its business, rivals, management, and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could TJX's shares go in the forecast?

paragraphs.text: The 2029 outcomes range from $115.98 to $191.65. The bear case has a 25% probability, the base case 55%, and the bull case 20%, because moderate continued growth is better supported than either sustained execution failure or a full operating acceleration.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for TJX's base case, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives $5,702 million initially and only $5,899 million by the final date. It assumes weak Marmaxx transactions, less favorable buying, and margin erosion. The bull case reaches $7,247 million because Marmaxx transactions recover, HomeGoods stays strong, and new stores add productive sales. Management’s 3%–4% comp outlook and raised adjusted EPS guidance support the base, while FY26’s outperformance supports confidence in execution.

blocks.heading: How much cash does TJX really make?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow means cash from operations after capital spending. Operating cash reached $6,874 million in FY26. Capital spending was $1,957 million, leaving $4,917 million of analytical free cash flow. That was about 90% of net income, which supports the quality of the reported profit.

Stock compensation adds back $214 million because no cash leaves immediately when shares are issued. But employees still receive value, and existing owners are diluted. Deducting it gives analytical “real free cash flow” of $4,703 million.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for TJX today?

paragraphs.text: Revenue and operating margin rose over five years, while TJX’s real free cash flow as a share of sales tests whether those profits convert to cash. Net cash stayed positive, but the latest quarter’s reported profit included a tariff-refund benefit. At $141.14, TJX trades at 26.09x trailing earnings and 26.78x next-twelve-month earnings; free cash flow yield is 3.2%, real free cash flow yield is 3.0%, dividend yield is 1.4%, and buyback yield is 1.6%.

blocks.heading: How much does TJX pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The base dividend starts at $1.92 per share, the stated FY27 amount, then grows 10% annually to $2.32. The bear freezes it at $1.92 after the first year, while the bull applies 13% annual growth and reaches $2.45. The base is below the recent dividend trend because capital spending and temporary benefits create less room for distribution. FY26 free cash flow of $4,917 million nevertheless supports continued increases.

blocks.heading: Is TJX's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: TJX used its cash in three broad ways: reinvestment, debt repayment and shareholder distributions. Across the five years ending January 2026, it generated $18,089 million of free cash flow and paid $19,515 million through dividends and buybacks. Payouts exceeded free cash flow in the earlier years, but coverage improved as operations recovered from pandemic disruption.

In FY2026, dividends took $1,842 million and buybacks took $2,522 million. TJX also received $311 million from issuing shares, principally through employee arrangements. Buybacks reduced outstanding shares from approximately 1,181 million to 1,107 million, though their value still depends on the price paid.

Free cash flow means cash from operations after capital spending. Operating cash reached $6,874 million in FY26. Capital spending was $1,957 million, leaving $4,917 million of analytical free cash flow. That was about 90% of net income, which supports the quality of the reported profit.

paragraphs.text: The view would move toward the bear case if FY27–FY28 Marmaxx transactions remain weak and comps fall below the 3%–4% plan. Higher buying costs, markdowns, or freight pressure in FY28–FY29 would reinforce that shift. By October 2029, slower earnings growth could drive the P/E toward 21x and restrict buybacks.

earnings.meta_description: TJX guides to adjusted EPS of $5.15–$5.20, 3.0%–4.0% comparable-sales growth and 12.0%–12.1% margin; results are due November 18, 2026.
earnings.opening: TJX’s next results are expected on November 18, 2026. Watch whether Marmaxx transactions recover.
earnings.closing: The full TJX memo also answers questions about TJX’s business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: What has TJX guided for FY27?

paragraphs.text: On August 19, TJX raised fiscal 2027 diluted earnings per share, or profit divided among shares including possible employee-issued shares, to $5.31–$5.36. Its adjusted range was $5.15–$5.20, excluding the net refund benefit.

Comparable sales measure growth at established stores. TJX still expects annual comparable-sales growth of 3.0%–4.0% and an adjusted pretax margin of 12.0%–12.1%. Because the sales target did not rise with the profit forecast, improvement must come partly from margins, buybacks or other efficiency.

blocks.heading: Has TJX kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Management also beat its fiscal 2026 promise. It had forecast comparable sales growth of 2%–3% and EPS of US$4.34–US$4.43. The year delivered 5% comparable growth and US$4.87 reported EPS; adjusted EPS was US$4.73 even after excluding a litigation-settlement benefit.

blocks.heading: What have TJX’s last eight quarters shown?

paragraphs.text: Revenue grew 5.4%, while operating income grew 22.7% and diluted EPS grew 23.6%. Profit therefore rose much faster than sales, but the cause was not simply better selling.
